legal.headline: Magistrate can take cognisance of private complaint only after examining complainant and hearing the accused: Delhi High Court
legal.hook: Magistrate can take cognisance of private complaint only after examining complainant and hearing the accused: Delhi High Court
legal.summary: The Delhi High Court has clarified the procedural requirements magistrates must follow before taking cognisance of a private complaint under the Indian Penal Code. A magistrate cannot summarily accept and register a private complaint; instead, the magistrate must first examine the complainant under oath, then provide the accused an opportunity to be heard before deciding whether cognisance should be taken. The court emphasized that skipping these procedural safeguards—particularly failing to hear the accused before taking cognisance—violates the accused's fundamental right to natural justice and renders the subsequent proceedings vulnerable to challenge. The judgment addresses a recurring gap in lower court practice where magistrates have been accepting private complaints and issuing summons without following the mandatory examination-and-hearing sequence prescribed by criminal procedure law.
legal.contextNote: This applies to Section 200–203 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, which mandate that before taking cognisance of a private complaint, a magistrate *must* examine the complainant on oath and record the substance of the examination, then grant the accused a reasonable opportunity to be heard (Section 202). The Delhi High Court's ruling aligns with existing precedent (*R.P. Sharma v. State of UP*, 1995) but directly targets magistrate-level non-compliance. (1) In-house counsel defending private complaints should immediately challenge any cognisance order that skips the Section 200–203 procedure; such orders are jurisdictionally defective and grounds for quashing. (2) Corporate entities facing private complaints (common in contractual disputes escalated to criminal complaints) should ensure counter-affidavits are filed at the examination stage, not after summons issue. (3) Compliance teams should flag private complaints to legal counsel *before* magistrate registration, as the examination window is the critical intervention point.
